children.text: A Ball on a Turntable

A ball of mass m, radius r and spherically symmetric mass distribution has inertia I about any central axis. It rolls without slipping on a horizontal turntable, assumed large enough that it never falls off. In the laboratory, its horizontal centre position is \(\mathbf R\), velocity \(\mathbf v\), and spin \(\boldsymbol\omega\). The turntable rotates about upward \(\hat{\mathbf z}\) at signed rate \(\Omega\). Initial \(\mathbf R_0,\mathbf v_0,\Omega_0\) are known, including vector directions. Write \(J\mathbf a=\hat{\mathbf z}\times\mathbf a\), \(\alpha=I/(I+mr^2)\), and \(\delta=I_d/(mr^2)\), where \(I_d\) is turntable inertia. Part A fixes \(\Omega=\Omega_0\). Part B lets the table rotate freely. Part C adds uniformly distributed surface charge Q and vertical uniform field \(\mathbf B=B\hat{\mathbf z}\), with B positive. Use the standard cross product. The source preamble has a typo in its z component.

Eliminate friction and spin to find the ball acceleration for constant table rate.

children.text: A Ball on a Turntable
A.1. Rolling constraint

The bottom contact velocity equals the local table velocity: \(\mathbf v-r\boldsymbol\omega\times\hat{\mathbf z}=\Omega\hat{\mathbf z}\times\mathbf R\). Thus \[\mathbf v=\Omega J\mathbf R+r\boldsymbol\omega\times\hat{\mathbf z}.\]
A.2. Ball acceleration

If friction is \(\mathbf F\), then \(m\dot{\mathbf v}=\mathbf F\) and \(I\dot{\boldsymbol\omega}=-rJ\mathbf F\). Differentiate the rolling constraint and eliminate friction to get \(\dot{\mathbf v}=\alpha\Omega J\mathbf v\).
A.3. Velocity-position relation
Constant \(\alpha\Omega\) allows direct integration: \[\mathbf v=\mathbf v_0+\alpha\Omega J(\mathbf R-\mathbf R_0).\]
A.4. Explicit trajectory

Put \(q=\alpha\Omega\). Then \[\mathbf R(t)=\mathbf R_0+\frac{\sin qt}{q}\mathbf v_0+\frac{1-\cos qt}{q}J\mathbf v_0.\] It is a circle of radius \(|\mathbf v_0/q|\), centred at \(\mathbf R_c=\mathbf R_0+J\mathbf v_0/q\). The q=0 limit is straight-line motion.
A.5. Return to a table mark

The ball-circle angular rate is \(q=2\Omega/7\). Both the ball and the mark certainly return together at \(t=14\pi/|\Omega|\). An earlier coincidence depends on the specified initial velocity direction and the second intersection of the two equal-radius circles. The source gives \(14\pi/(9|\Omega|)\) for a special crossing configuration, not a universal first-return time. To determine the actual earliest time for the given vectors solve \(\mathbf R(t)=\mathcal R(\Omega t)\mathbf R_0\) with the explicit A.4 trajectory. A tangent, coincident-circle or differently oriented initial geometry can change the earlier solutions.
B.1. Freely rotating constraint

Combining the rolling and spin equations still gives \[\dot{\mathbf v}=\alpha(\dot\Omega J\mathbf R+\Omega J\mathbf v).\] Integrating, \(\mathbf v=\alpha\Omega J\mathbf R+\mathbf c\), where \(\mathbf c=\mathbf v_0-\alpha\Omega_0J\mathbf R_0\) is constant.
B.2. Table angular acceleration

Table torque is \(I_d\dot\Omega=-m(\mathbf R\times\dot{\mathbf v})_z\). Substitution yields \[(I_d+\alpha mR^2)\dot\Omega=-\alpha m\Omega\,\mathbf c\cdot\mathbf R.\] This determines the sign as well as the magnitude.
B.3. Table speed versus radius

Since \(\mathbf c\cdot\mathbf R=\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf R=\tfrac12dR^2/dt\), integration gives \[\Omega^2=\Omega_0^2\frac{I_d+\alpha mR_0^2}{I_d+\alpha mR^2}.\] The sign of the rotation remains that of the initial rate when it is nonzero.
B.4. Maximum possible table speed
The denominator is smallest at R=0, giving \[|\Omega|_{max}=|\Omega_0|\sqrt{1+\alpha mR_0^2/I_d}.\] This is an upper bound. A particular trajectory need not pass through the centre.
B.5. Conic trajectories

Total vertical angular momentum is \(M_z=I_d\Omega+m(\mathbf R\times\mathbf v)_z+I\omega_z\). The last term is constant, so define \(L=M_z-I\omega_z\). With \(\mathbf c=c\hat{\mathbf x}\), \[L=\Omega(I_d+\alpha mR^2)-mcy.\] Put \(C=\Omega_0^2(I_d+\alpha mR_0^2)\). Combining with B.3 gives \[(L+mcy)^2=C[I_d+\alpha m(x^2+y^2)].\] This is a conic: ellipse if \(C\alpha m>m^2c^2\), parabola if equal, hyperbola if smaller, with degenerate cases separately possible. Squaring loses the sign constraint \(L+mcy=\Omega(I_d+\alpha mR^2)\), so retain the branch consistent with the initial data. Several signs and coefficient expansions in the source solution are inconsistent. The conserved-form equation avoids them.
C.1. Charged-ball equations

The uniform surface charge has magnetic moment \(\boldsymbol\mu=Qr^2\boldsymbol\omega/3\). Thus \[m\dot{\mathbf v}=\mathbf F+Q\mathbf v\times\mathbf B,\quad I\dot{\boldsymbol\omega}=-rJ\mathbf F+\frac{Qr^2}{3}\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf B.\]
C.2. Magnetic acceleration

Differentiate the rolling relation and substitute the C.1 equations. With \(A=I+mr^2\), \[A\ddot{\mathbf R}=\left(\frac{4Qr^2B}{3}-I\Omega\right)\dot{\mathbf R}\times\hat{\mathbf z}-\frac{Qr^2B\Omega}{3}\mathbf R.\] Every coefficient retains the signed table rate and charge.
C.3. Removing the gyroscopic term

\[\gamma=\frac{4Qr^2B/3-I\Omega}{I+mr^2},\qquad\beta=\frac{Qr^2B\Omega}{3(I+mr^2)}.\] The numerator of beta includes Omega, omitted in one source line. A rotating-frame substitution with \(\eta=-\gamma t/2+\phi\) gives \(\ddot\rho+\beta_{\mathrm{prime}}\rho=0\), \(\beta_{\mathrm{prime}}=\beta+\gamma^2/4\), for solutions with a fixed direction in that rotating frame. More generally the two rotating Cartesian components each satisfy that oscillator equation. Positive beta prime gives harmonic components, zero gives linear components, negative gives exponential components. A general polar radius also has an angular-momentum term, so the scalar radial form is not universal.
C.4. Expanding spiral

The initial phase rate is -1, so \(\gamma=2\), while \(\beta=-1\). The solution is \[x=(1+t)\cos t,\qquad y=-(1+t)\sin t.\] It spirals clockwise with linearly increasing radius. For \(I=mr^2/10\), \(\alpha=1/11\) and \(\gamma=4\beta/\Omega-\alpha\Omega\), so \(\Omega=-11\pm\sqrt{77}\). Both table rates are negative. Since beta is proportional to Q times Omega and B is positive, Q is positive. The source says negative, contradicting its own beta formula. Initial data alone do not determine beta and gamma without the specified linearly growing case.
C.5. Spiral energy growth

For \(\rho=1+t\), \(v^2=1+\rho^2\). The horizontal spin from rolling is \(\boldsymbol\omega_h=J\mathbf v+\Omega\mathbf R\), so \(\omega_h^2=1+(1+\Omega)^2\rho^2\). Vertical spin is constant. Thus \[\Delta E=\tfrac12[1+I(1+\Omega)^2][(1+t)^2-1].\] At \(t\simeq2\pi N\), \(\Delta E\simeq2\pi^2N^2[1+(1+\Omega)^2/11]\), with per-revolution increment \(\simeq4\pi^2N[1+(1+\Omega)^2/11]\). The source replaces the signed factor by \((1+|\Omega|)^2\), which is inconsistent with the rolling constraint for the clockwise spiral. Its explicit inertia 1/11 also differs from the earlier 1/10 mass distribution. Treat this part as a local changed-inertia evaluation. If recomputing C.4 for I=1/11, use \(\alpha=1/12\) and \(\Omega=-12\pm4\sqrt6\).
